normalized.governing_thought: Launch Copilot in Q4 2027, after the mobile rewrite, in a $12-a-seat Pro plan, not a $149 add-on
executive_summary: Customers value Copilot, but only about one in seven will pay for it as an add-on
– Beta volunteers gained 9 percentage points more output per dispatcher-hour than matched accounts
– Only 14% of beta accounts paid $149 a month, against 46% stated intent
A Pro plan at $12 more per seat with a request allowance beats the add-on within the margin floor
– The add-on yields about $0.85M of gross profit a year, not $8M of ARR
– Pro adds $2.9M of ARR and reaches 2.4 times as many accounts
Routewise's AI is a smaller threat than claimed; mobile reliability loses far more customers
– Even the whole win-rate fall is worth at most $0.64M of ARR a year
– Mobile reliability drives 27% of churn, against 6% for AI features
Shipping the mobile rewrite first protects about twice the ARR that waiting on Copilot risks
– A mobile slip risks up to $1.09M of ARR, against $0.56M for Copilot
– A Q4 2027 Pro launch still closes the NRR gap if 26% of accounts move
Approve Pro now, test its price, and launch in Q4 2027 unless the win rate says AI cannot wait
– A win rate still near 37% after the discount would bring the launch forward

slides.title: Customers value Copilot, but few pay $149 for it
Customers value Copilot, but only about one in seven will pay for it as a separate add-on

claims.claim: The productivity gain is real among beta volunteers but unproven for a typical customer, whose use is far lighter
evidence: 9 pp more gain in jobs per dispatcher-hour than matched accounts

claims.claim: When asked to pay $149 a month, few beta accounts did, and both demand readings lean on larger accounts
evidence: 14% of beta accounts bought in the paywall test, against 46% stated intent

claims.claim: Copilot is worth selling, but the price must reach the many light users, not only the few heavy ones

slides.title: 1a: Copilot's gain is proven only among volunteers: 9 percentage points more output per dispatcher-hour

claims.claim: 4.1 dispatcher hours saved a week, self-reported
evidence: Reported by beta users, not measured in the product
No matched figure, so there is no baseline to compare with
A direction, not a number to price on

claims.claim: 9 pp more gain in jobs per dispatcher-hour than matched accounts
evidence: Beta accounts: +11% against their prior 12 weeks
Matched non-beta accounts: +2% over the same weeks
The only measured productivity effect in the beta

claims.claim: 4 pp higher three-month renewal than matched accounts
evidence: 97% for beta accounts against 93% for matched ones
A short window that cannot show annual churn
Volunteers who chose to try Copilot renew more anyway

claims.claim: Before pricing on productivity, measure the gain in a random sample of accounts that did not volunteer
evidence: Beta accounts volunteered; they average 8.1 seats against 6.2 for all accounts and are more active than the base
240 volunteer accounts compared with matched non-beta accounts, 12-week beta

slides.title: 1a: A few heavy accounts drive Copilot use: a top-tenth account makes four times the requests of the average one

claims.claim: Use is skewed toward a small group of heavy accounts
evidence: Requests a month: Median account 1900; Mean account 3600; Paywall buyers 6800; Top 10% of accounts 14500
4.03x requests of a top-10% account compared with the mean account
Median, 1,900 requests: half of the beta accounts use less, and the mean sits 1.9 times above the median
Top 10%: together they generated 58% of all AI requests in the beta

claims.claim: the accounts that paid were the heavy users, not the typical ones
evidence: Paywall buyers, 6,800 requests

slides.title: 1b: Paid demand is under a third of stated intent, with 14% of beta accounts buying against 46% in the survey

claims.claim: Stated intent overstates paid demand
evidence: Share at $149 per account a month: Survey: likely to buy 0.46; Paywall test: bought 0.14
3.3x survey intent compared with paid take-up
Survey, 46%: intent from the 610 admins who chose to reply, not a purchase
Paywall, 14%: 17 of 120 beta accounts paid once the free period ended, a real buying decision

claims.claim: Even 14% is a ceiling: the buyers came from volunteers, who are larger and more active than the base

slides.title: 1b: Both demand readings come from accounts larger than the typical customer, which puts true take-up below 14%

claims.claim: Both demand readings come from accounts larger than the typical customer, which puts true take-up below 14%
evidence: All accounts: 6.2 seats, Base, take-up not measured; The population the price must work for
Beta and paywall accounts: 8.1 seats, 1.3x, 14%; Volunteers, more active than the base
Survey respondents: 9.4 seats, 1.5x, 46%; Largest bias / Only 6% of admins replied, from accounts half as large again as the base
Survey sent to all 9,800 account admins in October 2026; 610 replied

slides.title: Customers value Copilot, but few pay $149 for it
A Pro plan at $12 more per seat is the strongest package, ahead of the add-on and of a free feature

claims.claim: Add-on, per account ($149 per account a month): Reject: few, heavy buyers (2a, 2b)
Pro plan, per seat ($12 per seat a month): Launch, with a request allowance (2c)
Free in Core (No charge): Reject: margin below the 75% floor (2d)
evidence: Team assessment from slides 2a–2d; full circle = strongest of the three packages
Revenue and margin ratings follow the first-year sizing on the next slides; fit with market reflects Routewise including AI in its Pro plan

slides.title: 2a: The add-on's realistic first year is $0.85M of gross profit, not the $8M of ARR in the proposal

claims.claim: Three corrections take the case from $8M to under $1M
evidence: Waterfall ($M): Survey case, 46% buy 8.0603; Paid take-up of 14% 5.6072 reduction (to 2.4531); Inference 1.0076; Platform and support 0.6; Gross profit 0.8455
Paid take-up: 14% bought in the paywall test, under a third of the survey's 46% (1b)
Inference: buyers average 6,800 requests, so each costs about $61 a month to serve
1,372 buyers, 14% of all × $1,788 price a year = $2.5M ARR − $1.01M inference − $0.6M platform = $0.8M gross profit

claims.claim: Result: the add-on runs at about a 34% gross margin, against 78% for the company

slides.title: 2b: Heavy users would erode a flat add-on: a top-tenth account costs about $131 a month to serve against a $149 price

claims.claim: A flat price invites the heaviest users
evidence: Inference cost a month at $0.009 a request: Median account 17.1; Mean account 32.4; Paywall buyers 61.2; Top 10% of accounts 130.5; Add-on price 149
87.6% of the $149 price goes to inference for a top-10% account
Buyers: the accounts that paid average 6,800 requests, so inference takes 41% of what they pay
No link to use: a per-account price rises with neither seats nor requests
No relief before 2028: the $0.009 price is fixed through December 2027

slides.title: 2b: A pooled allowance of about 1,330 requests per seat keeps Pro's AI cost below the $12 each seat pays

claims.claim: A pooled allowance of about 1,330 requests per seat keeps Pro's AI cost below the $12 each seat pays
evidence: $12 per seat a month ÷ $0.01 per request = 1,333.3 requests per seat a month at which inference equals the price
1,333.3 ÷ 444.4 requests per seat used by the mean beta account (3,600 over 8.1 seats) = 3x headroom over today's typical use

claims.claim: Most accounts would never reach the allowance; heavy ones pay for packs
evidence: The allowance is pooled across an account's seats, so light and heavy users offset each other
Use above the allowance is sold in request packs priced above $0.009 a request
A top-10% account (14,500 requests a month) exceeds the pool only below about 11 seats

claims.claim: Set the final allowance below the break-even of 1,333 once the price test shows real use

slides.title: 2c: Pro would add about $2.9M of ARR and $1.0M of gross profit a year if take-up matches the 2023 tier

claims.claim: Pro would add about $2.9M of ARR and $1.0M of gross profit a year
evidence: 3,234 accounts moving: 33% of 9,800, as with the 2023 tier × $892.8 per account a year ($12 × 6.2 seats × 12) = $2.9M Pro ARR in the first year − $1.9M inference at mean beta use plus $0.6M platform = $1.03M Pro gross profit a year

claims.claim: The case rests on the 2023 tier precedent, not on survey intent
evidence: 33% of accounts move to Pro within a year, as with the 2023 higher tier
Accounts that move average 6.2 seats, like the base
Pro accounts use Copilot like the mean beta account: 3,600 requests a month at $0.009 (conservative: beta accounts are larger and more active)
$0.6M a year of platform, evaluation and support cost

slides.title: 2c: Pro beats the add-on on revenue, reach and price for the average account

claims.claim: Pro earns more ARR, even against the add-on's ceiling
evidence: ARR added, $M, first year: Add-on 2.4531; Pro 2.8873
$2.9M Pro ARR at 33% take-up (2c) ÷ $2.5M add-on ARR at 14% take-up (2a) = 1.2x

claims.claim: Pro reaches more than twice as many accounts
evidence: Accounts paying, first year: Add-on 1372; Pro 3234

claims.claim: Pro costs an average account half as much
evidence: Price increase, 6.2-seat account, $ a month: Add-on 149; Pro 74.4
The add-on adds 30% to an average account's $490 monthly Core bill; Pro adds 15%

claims.claim: Pro pays back its $1.47M of engineering in about 17 months, against about 21 for the add-on
evidence: Payback = 14 engineers × $210,000 × half a year ÷ gross profit a year

slides.title: 2d: Copilot has to be paid for: giving it away in Core would cut gross margin to 73.5%, below the 75% floor

claims.claim: Only paid packages hold the floor
evidence: Company gross margin: Add-on at $149 0.7622; Pro with allowance 0.7598; Pro without allowance 0.7413; Free in Core 0.7347; Margin floor 0.75
Free in Core: even at median use, $2.0M of inference and no new revenue
Pro without allowance: if Pro attracts users as heavy as the paywall buyers, margin falls to 74.1%
Pro with allowance: 76.0%, close to the add-on, with more than twice the reach (2c)
$44.9M gross profit today − $2.01M inference − $0.6M platform = $42.3M new profit ÷ $57.6M ARR = 73.5% margin
Margins = (today's gross profit + package gross profit) ÷ (ARR + package ARR); Pro without allowance uses 6,800 requests a month per account

slides.title: Customers value Copilot, but few pay $149 for it
Routewise's AI is a smaller threat than the sales memo claims, and AI features explain little of our churn

claims.claim: The win-rate fall coincides with a Routewise discount, and even if AI caused all of it the loss is modest
evidence: $0.6M new ARR a year at most, if AI caused the whole fall
109.2 deals a year lost to the fall of 7 pp × $5,877.6 ARR per average account = $0.6M ceiling on new ARR lost

claims.claim: Customers leave over mobile reliability far more often than over missing AI features
evidence: 4.5x mobile-reliability churn compared with AI-feature churn

slides.title: 3a: AI may not explain our lower win rate against Routewise: a first-year discount ran alongside its AI launch

claims.claim: Two causes overlap in one quarter
evidence: Win rate in deals where Routewise competed: Q1–Q2 2026 0.44; Q3 2026 0.37
109.2 deals a year lost at the lower win rate, out of 1,560 where Routewise competes
Q3 2026: Routewise put AI in its Pro plan in September and offered 20% off the first year in the same quarter
Loss notes: 31% mention AI features, but a mention is not the main reason for a loss
Loss notes cover all Q3 2026 lost deals, not only those against Routewise

claims.claim: The test: a Q4 win rate still near 37% after the discount would point to AI

slides.title: 3a: Winning back every deal lost since Routewise's launch is worth $0.64M of ARR a year, a third of the memo's figure

claims.claim: ceiling on new ARR lost a year is $0.6M
evidence: 1,560 deals a year where Routewise competes: 2,600 × 60% × 7 pp fall in win rate, 44% to 37% = 109.2 deals a year lost to the fall
109.2 × $5,877.6 per account a year (6.2 seats × $79 × 12) = $0.6M
Upper bound: the whole fall from 44% to 37% is caused by Routewise's AI, none by its 20% first-year discount

claims.claim: Even the ceiling is a third of the sales memo's claim
evidence: The memo's claim, a third of the 983 deals lost where Routewise competes, would be $1.9M, three times this ceiling
31% of loss notes mention AI, but mentions are not causes

slides.title: 3b: Mobile app reliability drives 27% of churn, 4.5 times as much as missing AI features

claims.claim: Customers leave over the app Copilot would delay
evidence: Main reason for leaving, % of churned accounts, 2026 (n = 1,190): Mobile app reliability 0.27; Price 0.22; Other 0.16; Missing integrations 0.15; Went out of business or sold 0.14; Switched for AI features 0.06
4.5x mobile-reliability churn compared with AI-feature churn
Mobile, 27%: the largest reason, and the rewrite that a Q2 Copilot launch would push back
AI features, 6%: fifth of six reasons, behind price and missing integrations
Requests agree: 38% rank a reliable mobile app first, twice the 19% for AI scheduling

slides.title: 3b: Fixing mobile reliability is worth up to 3.8 percentage points of NRR a year, against 0.8 for AI features

claims.claim: $2.2M ARR / 3.8 pp of NRR lost a year to mobile-reliability churn
evidence: 1,372 accounts churn a year: 14% of 9,800
27% of them leave mainly over mobile reliability
Each is worth $5,878 of ARR on average
Almost the whole gap of 4 percentage points to 105%
Recovered only if the rewrite fixes reliability

claims.claim: $0.5M ARR / 0.8 pp of NRR lost a year to AI-feature churn
evidence: 6% of churned accounts left for AI features
The most Copilot could win back from churn
A fifth of the NRR gap at most

claims.claim: Copilot's case rests on revenue, not on retention
evidence: Upper bounds: assume every churned account is worth the average ARR and the fix removes all churn of that reason

slides.title: Customers value Copilot, but few pay $149 for it
Shipping the mobile rewrite first protects about twice the ARR that waiting two quarters for Copilot puts at risk

claims.claim: Shipping the mobile rewrite first protects about twice the ARR that waiting two quarters for Copilot puts at risk
evidence: $1.1M ARR at risk if the mobile rewrite slips two quarters (4a) ÷ $0.6M ARR at risk if Copilot waits two quarters: lost deals plus AI churn (4a) = 1.9x

claims.claim: Both sides are upper bounds built the same way
evidence: Upper bound on both sides: the mobile rewrite removes all mobile-reliability churn, and Copilot removes all AI-feature churn and the whole win-rate fall
Two quarters of delay, valued as half a year of each annual loss
Churned and lost accounts are worth the average Core account, $5,878 of ARR a year
If the rewrite goes first, Copilot launches two quarters later, in Q4 2027, when the 14 engineers are free

claims.claim: Keep the 14 engineers on the mobile rewrite and launch Pro with Copilot in Q4 2027

slides.title: 4a: Mobile churn is the largest risk of delay: up to $1.09M of ARR if the rewrite slips two quarters

claims.claim: The mobile slip costs more than Copilot's wait
evidence: ARR at risk ($M): Mobile churn, rewrite slips 1.0886; Routewise deals, Copilot waits 0.3209; AI churn, Copilot waits 0.2419
$2.2M ARR lost a year to mobile churn (3b) × 0.5 two quarters of delay = $1.1M ARR at risk from the slip
Mobile risk relative to both Copilot risks 1.9x: $1.09M ÷ ($0.32M + $0.24M)
Mobile: 27% of churners leave over reliability; two more quarters of that churn is the largest single risk
Routewise deals: a ceiling, since the discount may explain the fall (3a)

claims.claim: Pro revenue is delayed, not lost: its $1.4M of half-year revenue still arrives, two quarters later

slides.title: 4a: Mobile first delays Copilot by two quarters but keeps both priorities inside the 2028 target window

claims.claim: Mobile first delays Copilot by two quarters but keeps both priorities inside the 2028 target window
evidence: Mobile app rewrite: Copilot first – Slips two quarters; Mobile first – Ships on the current plan; Mobile first wins
Copilot in Pro: Q2 2027 vs Q4 2027, when the 14 engineers are free; Copilot first wins

Pro upgrades before end-2028: Six quarters vs Four quarters, the year the 2023 tier needed; Both enough
Inference price: $0.009 a request, fixed through December 2027 vs Same; renegotiation at launch; Neutral

Assumes Copilot follows the rewrite two quarters later; to be confirmed with engineering

slides.title: 4b: Launched in Q4 2027, Pro still closes the NRR gap on its own if at least 26% of accounts move

claims.claim: Pro still closes the NRR gap on its own if at least 26% of accounts move
evidence: $2.3M extra expansion ARR needed: 4 pp of $57.6M ARR ÷ $8.7M Pro ARR if every account moved: 9,800 × $892.80 = 26.3% share of accounts that must move to Pro

claims.claim: The 2023 tier cleared this bar within a year
evidence: The 2023 higher tier reached 33% of accounts within a year
Pro upgrades count as expansion in NRR; churn and other expansion stay at 2026 levels

Fixing mobile reliability would add up to 3.8 percentage points on top (3b)

slides.title: Next steps

normalized.recommendation: Launch Copilot in Q4 2027, after the mobile rewrite, in a $12-a-seat Pro plan, not a $149 add-on. Approve Pro now, test its price, and launch in Q4 2027 unless the win rate says AI cannot wait (keep the 14 engineers on the mobile rewrite; pooled request allowance plus request packs; bring the launch forward only if the win rate stays down after the discount).

alternatives_considered.option: Add-on at $149 per account a month (the Q2 add-on proposal)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Reject: few, heavy buyers (2a, 2b). Realistic first year is $0.85M of gross profit, not the $8M of ARR in the proposal; runs at about a 34% gross margin; top-10% account costs about $131 a month to serve against $149.

alternatives_considered.option: Pro plan at $12 more per seat with a request allowance
alternatives_considered.treatment: Chosen: Launch, with a request allowance (2c). Adds about $2.9M of ARR and $1.0M of gross profit; reaches more than twice as many accounts; company margin 76.0%.
Reject: margin below the 75% floor (2d); would cut gross margin to 73.5%.
If Pro attracts users as heavy as the paywall buyers, margin falls to 74.1%, below the floor.

alternatives_considered.option: Copilot first, Q2 2027 (mobile rewrite slips two quarters)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected in favour of mobile first: $1.1M ARR at risk vs $0.6M; Copilot first wins only on Copilot timing. Launch would be brought forward only if the Q4 2026 win rate stays near 37% after the discount.
Chosen: protects about twice the ARR; keeps both priorities inside the 2028 target window.
Left out: the provider price is fixed through December 2027; revisit at renewal.
Left out: out of scope, the decision is about Copilot; price already drives 22% of churn.
Left out: the brief fixes engineering at 60 in total and gives no hiring data.

assumptions_and_uncertainties: Add-on take-up: 14% of accounts, a ceiling (paywall test among beta volunteers)
Pro take-up: 33% of accounts within a year (2023 higher-tier launch)
Seats per moving account: 6.2, like the base
Pro usage: 3,600 requests a month per account (mean beta account, conservative)
Inference price: $0.009 a request, fixed in the contract through December 2027
Running cost: $0.6M a year (platform, evaluation and support)
Account value: $5,878 of ARR a year (6.2 seats × $79 × 12 months)
Copilot timing if mobile goes first: Q4 2027, two quarters later; our assumption; confirm with engineering
Mobile rewrite dates assume the current plan finishes in Q2 2027 with the 14 engineers; to be confirmed with engineering

ARR-at-risk and churn-cost figures are upper bounds: every churned account is worth the average ARR and the fix removes all churn of that reason; Copilot removes all AI-feature churn and the whole win-rate fall
Two quarters of delay valued as half a year of each annual loss
Pro upgrades count as expansion in NRR; churn and other expansion stay at 2026 levels
Productivity gain is proven only among volunteers; hours saved are self-reported; beta accounts average 8.1 seats vs 6.2 and are more active
Churn reasons: one reason per account; self-reported
Loss notes: a mention is not a cause; cover all lost deals, not only those against Routewise
Win-rate fall may be caused by Routewise's 20% first-year discount rather than AI
Inference price fall of 35% at renewal is an upside from 2028, not part of the base case
Risks: win rate keeps falling; Pro take-up below 26%; heavy use above the allowance; gain fails outside volunteers; mobile rewrite slips anyway
